If your Social Security deposit landed in your bank account this month and the number looked off, you're not imagining things. Benefit amounts can shift from month to month for reasons that have nothing to do with a cut to Social Security itself. Most of the time, a smaller check traces back to a handful of routine, built-in factors — things like Medicare premiums, tax withholding, or a prior overpayment. None of these mean something is broken. But they're not always explained clearly, which leaves a lot of beneficiaries confused when the deposit doesn't match what they expected. Here's a closer look at what's likely going on. Now Available: The Definitive Guide to Retirement Income Many successful investors eventually reach the same moment. The saving is done, the portfolio is built, and the question quietly changes from how much can I grow this to how much can I take out? Get that second question wrong and decades of good investing can come apart in a handful of years. That is exactly what The Definitive Guide to Retirement Income helps answer. 1

Read More Here › SPONSORED Medicare Part B premiums can take a bigger bite For most retirees, the Medicare Part B premium is deducted directly from their Social Security payment before it ever reaches their bank account. These premiums typically adjust every January, and when the new amount kicks in, it can make a check look smaller compared to the prior December's payment, even though your underlying Social Security benefit didn't shrink. Medicare.gov publishes the current standard Part B premium each year, and it's worth checking your most recent Medicare notice to confirm the exact amount being withheld from your payment. IRMAA surcharges can raise your Medicare costs Beyond the standard premium, some beneficiaries pay an income-related monthly adjustment amount, known as IRMAA. This surcharge applies to people whose income, based on tax returns from two years prior, exceeds certain thresholds set by the Social Security Administration (SSA) and the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services. Because IRMAA is based on older tax data, a surcharge can show up even if your current income has dropped, for example, after retiring or losing a spouse. If a one-time event like a home sale or retirement account withdrawal pushed your income higher two years ago, it could be affecting your premium now. The SSA does notify beneficiaries of IRMAA determinations by mail, but it's easy to miss or forget about that letter months later. The earnings test can reduce benefits if you're still working If you claimed Social Security before reaching full retirement age (FRA) — the age at which you qualify for 100% of your benefit, which is 67 for people born in 1960 or later — and you're still working, your benefit may be subject to the retirement earnings test. For 2026, the SSA will withhold $1 in benefits for every $2 earned above $24,480 per year for people who are under FRA all year, according to the SSA. In the year you reach FRA, a higher limit applies: $65,160 for 2026, with $1 withheld for every $3 earned above that amount, only counting earnings before the month you reach FRA. Once you reach full retirement age, this test no longer applies, and any benefits withheld earlier are generally recalculated into a higher monthly payment going forward. If you're working and claiming early, this withholding is one of the most common reasons a check comes in lower than the number you were expecting. Learn More Here › SPONSORED Voluntary tax withholding can shrink your deposit Social Security benefits can be subject to federal income tax, depending on your total income. Many beneficiaries choose to have taxes withheld directly from their monthly payment, using IRS Form W-4V, rather than paying a lump sum at tax time. If you elected voluntary withholding, or recently changed your withholding percentage, that adjustment will show up as a smaller net deposit. It's worth checking whether a withholding election, rather than any change to your actual benefit, explains the difference. Overpayment recovery can reduce or pause your payment If the SSA determines it paid you too much in a prior period, due to an income change, a processing error, or unreported information, it can recover that overpayment by withholding part or all of future payments. The agency is required to notify beneficiaries in writing before this happens and to explain the amount owed and the options available, including requesting a lower withholding rate or appealing the overpayment determination. Because these notices can arrive separately from the payment itself, it's possible to see a reduced deposit before fully connecting it to an overpayment letter received earlier. A COLA increase doesn't always mean a bigger net check Each January, the SSA applies a cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) to help benefits keep pace with inflation. For 2026, the SSA announced a 2.8% COLA, raising the average retirement benefit by about $56 a month to roughly $2,071, according to the SSA. But a COLA increase can also push some beneficiaries' income higher, which may, in turn, trigger a higher Medicare Part B premium or move someone into a new IRMAA bracket. In those cases, part or all of the COLA raise can be offset by higher Medicare costs, so the net deposit increase ends up smaller than the announced COLA percentage might suggest. Retirement News: Almost 80% of Americans fear a retirement age increase — here’s the real reason why Where to go when the numbers still don't add up Not every Social Security deduction is communicated clearly in advance, and it's understandable to feel caught off guard. The SSA recommends logging into your personal Social Security account online, where you can review your benefit verification letter, payment history, and any notices related to Medicare premiums or overpayments. If the discrepancy still isn't clear after checking your account, contacting the SSA directly at 1-800-772-1213 can help clarify which deduction applied and why. Bottom line A smaller-than-expected Social Security check is rarely a sign that something has gone wrong with the program itself. More often, it reflects one of a few routine, documented adjustments, like a Medicare premium change, an IRMAA bracket shift, earnings-test withholding, tax elections, or overpayment recovery, that are already built into how benefits are administered. Reviewing your Social Security account regularly and keeping any SSA or Medicare notices you receive can make it easier to catch these changes before they're a surprise. If the lower payment leaves a gap in your budget, you can look into ways to supplement your Social Security income . For anyone still unsure why a deposit looks different this month, SSA representatives can walk through the specific deductions applied to an individual account. FAQs How much can Social Security withhold to recover an overpayment? For most new Title II overpayments, which cover retirement, survivor, and disability benefits, SSA's default is to withhold 50% of your monthly benefit. That default applies to overpayment notices sent on or after April 25, 2025. SSA generally gives you roughly 90 days after the notice to ask for a lower withholding rate (Form SSA-634), a waiver (Form SSA-632), or an appeal of the overpayment (Form SSA-561) before withholding starts. A waiver request has no filing deadline. Can I appeal an IRMAA surcharge if my income dropped? Yes, if the drop came from a qualifying life-changing event. You file Form SSA-44 and ask SSA to use more recent income instead of the tax return from two years ago. Qualifying events include marriage, divorce, death of a spouse, work stoppage or reduction, loss of income-producing property, loss of pension income, and an employer settlement payment. A one-time income spike from a home sale or retirement account withdrawal generally isn't a qualifying event on its own, though it can raise your premium. How do I have federal income tax withheld from my Social Security? Social Security doesn't withhold tax unless you ask. You do that by filing IRS Form W-4V with SSA and choosing a flat percentage of each payment: 7%, 10%, 12%, or 22%. No other percentages are offered, and the amount withheld comes out before your deposit, which makes your net payment smaller. If you're not sure whether any of your benefit is taxable, check the amount against your combined income first.
